newsitem.title: MEXICO: Drug czar smooths path for Clinton visit to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Drug czar smooths path for Clinton visit to Mexico.

text.p: Smoothing over strained cross-border relations ahead of U.S. President Bill Clinton's visit here next month, U.S. drug czar Barry McCaffrey on Thursday heaped praise on Mexican officials for their role in the drug war.

"It is the U.S. belief that Mexican successes in the struggle against drugs this past year are a result of firm resolve at the top level of the Mexican government to stop drug trafficking and production," McCaffrey said in a speech to Mexican diplomats.

The brief overnight trip, in which McCaffrey was whisked in and out of the capital under heavy guard, came as top Mexican officials and ordinary citizens have blasted the United States recently over deep differences on drugs and immigration.
The U.S. "certification" process in March, in which Clinton and the U.S. Congress took highly public turns determining whether Mexico was an aid-worthy partner in the drug war, most angered Mexicans.

Clinton, who is due to visit Mexico City May 5-7, has battled with Congress over its harsh stance toward Mexico as corruptly permissive of drug traffickers, but has joined Congress in cracking down on illegal immigration.

On top of those issues, many Mexicans were chafing at unconfirmed media reports that the United States had presented Mexico a list of up to 50 most wanted drug traffickers to be extradited to the United States for trial.

"I want to be clear: this list doesn't exist," McCaffrey told a news conference, attempting to calm Mexican rage over what, if true, would be seen here as a heavy-handed violation of Mexican sovereignty.

McCaffrey, a former general who coordinates White House drug policy, met with top Mexican officials on Wednesday including his counterpart, Mariano Herran, Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria and Attorney General Jorge Madrazo.

McCaffrey stressed that demand for drugs in the United States is the root cause of the international problem and that joint cooperation "fully recognising the sovereign rights of each nation" was the only way to succeed.
He said 12 million U.S. citizens spend $50 billion a year consuming some kind of illegal drug, causing 14,000 deaths a year.
